bracket: [Textbook misprint: two printing defects in this stem, neither of which changes the answer. (i) The hydroxide ion is printed as \(\mathrm{OH(aq)}\), with NO negative charge; it should be \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}(aq)}\), since the equation must balance in charge as well as in atoms and the book itself writes \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) with its charge on the same line. Preserved as printed. (ii) The state symbol on water is typeset as an ITALIC DIGIT ONE, so the page reads \(\mathrm{H_2O(1)}\); confirmed from the PDF's own font data, where the character is the digit 1 in Times New Roman Italic. It is plainly the italic letter \(l\) for liquid, and is transcribed here as \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) because "(1)" is not a state symbol at all and would read as nonsense.]

[Textbook misprint: the book labels its FOURTH option "c." as well as its third, so the printed page reads "a. adding \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)  b. removing NO / c. adding NOCl  c. removal of \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)" — the letter c twice and no d at all. Verified on the printed page at magnification. The four option TEXTS are distinct and are stored here in the printed order as (a) to (d); only the duplicated letter is corrected, and the answer is unaffected.]

[Textbook misprint: as printed, NO option is strictly correct. The reaction \(\mathrm{A(g)} + \mathrm{B(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{C(g)} + \mathrm{D(g)}\) has 2 moles of gas on the left and 3 on the right, so \(\Delta n = +1\) and this chapter's own Eq. 12.7 gives \(K_P = K_C(RT)\), i.e. \(K_p/K_c = RT\), not 1. Option (d) is the answer intended and is what the general relation gives whenever \(\Delta n = 0\), which is very likely how the question was written — counting two species on each side rather than the moles. Separately, option (a) is printed as "\(K_c = \mathrm{Y}k_p\)", with a capital letter Y carrying no overbar, against option (c) on the same line which carries a proper radical sign; it is evidently a misprint for \(K_c = \sqrt{K_p}\), which would make options (a) and (b) the same statement rearranged and so rule out both. Both defects preserved as printed.]

[Textbook misprint: carbon is printed as a GAS, \(\mathrm{C(g)}\). This is the water-gas reaction, in which carbon is a solid, and the state symbol here is answer-affecting. As printed there are 2 moles of gas on each side, \(\Delta n = 0\), and a change of volume cannot move the equilibrium — which is the answer keyed above, since the rule of this bank is to solve the question exactly as the book prints it. With \(\mathrm{C(s)}\), the solid would be left out of the equilibrium expression, the gaseous moles would run 1 to 2, and increasing the volume would shift the equilibrium from left to right, making the option that reads "shift from left to right" the correct one instead. Preserved as printed, with both readings stated in the solution.]
